subtype: Approach: task decomposition with a shared board [Action]
passage:
Subject: Project plan, first update

Dear Irfan Sir,

Our team of four met on Saturday and cut the project into four parts: data collection, the model, the interface and the report. Each part became a set of small cards on one online board, and every card carries a name and a date. I took the interface, Meena took the data, and the other two took the model and the report. We agreed to look at the board together for ten minutes every Tuesday and Friday. After two weeks, nine of fourteen cards have moved to done, and two late cards were noticed early. Could we show you the board on Friday?

Regards,
Nazia

qa.q: How many cards had moved to done after two weeks?
qa.a: Nine of fourteen cards have moved to done.

qa.q: What is Nazia feeling as the update is written?
qa.a: Nazia seems proud and hopeful: the progress is reported with numbers, and asking to show the board suggests confidence.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the team use if cards keep slipping, and why?
qa.a: They could hold a short root-cause talk about the slipping cards, because a board shows what is late but not why it is late.

qa.q: How might Irfan Sir see this update?
qa.a: Irfan Sir gets a clear picture of who is doing what and when, so he can judge progress quickly and offer help early.

grounding: Shows a team breaking a project into parts, giving each card an owner and a date, and checking progress briefly twice weekly.

passage: On the whiteboard in the project lab, Rehana drew four boxes and started joining them with arrows. "Look," she said, tapping. "Nothing can train until the pipeline is running. So model training waits for Uday's pipeline. But the interface only needs a fake output for now, so Sharath can start it today." Uday, who owned the pipeline, glanced up from his laptop. "So I'm the bottleneck." "For a week or two, yes," said Rehana. "So the rest of us help you first: I'll write the cleaning script, Sharath will test the loader." She circled the pipeline box in red. "This is the critical path. If it slips, everything slips." Uday exhaled, and pulled a chair for Sharath.

qa.q: Who owned the pipeline?
qa.a: Uday owned the pipeline.

qa.q: What is Uday feeling when Rehana says the pipeline is the critical path?
qa.a: Uday feels the pressure of being the bottleneck, then some relief as Uday exhales and pulls a chair for Sharath because help is coming.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the team use to avoid waiting on one person, and why?
qa.a: They could agree on a simple fake data file for the model people to use meanwhile, because parallel work continues even before the real pipeline is ready.

qa.q: How does Sharath see this plan?
qa.a: Sharath can start the interface today with a fake output and also helps by testing the loader, so Sharath is neither idle nor blocked.

grounding: Shows dependency thinking in a team: the pipeline must come first, other parts can run in parallel, and the pipeline owner gets help.

passage: In the computer lab, Sharmila taped a sheet to the wall: "Week 3: something that works." Her teammate Jaya frowned at it. "But we planned face recognition." "That comes later," said Sharmila. "First, a rough but running attendance system. A student's name goes in, a tick goes into a table, a teacher can see it. Nothing fancy." For three weeks they built only that, taking turns at the keyboard. On day 21 they clicked through it for their guide, and it worked, though the screen looked plain. "Now the face part," said Jaya, and this time she sounded sure. Even if the semester ran short, there was already a demo to show. Sharmila took the sheet down and wrote "Week 4: faces" beneath.

qa.q: What did Sharmila tape to the wall?
qa.a: She taped a sheet reading 'Week 3: something that works.'

qa.q: What is Jaya feeling when she first sees the sheet?
qa.a: Jaya feels doubtful and a bit disappointed, frowning because they had planned face recognition.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Sharmila and Jaya use if they still feel unsure about starting simple, and why?
qa.a: They could sketch the full design on paper first and mark the smallest working slice, because that keeps the big plan visible while still delivering a demo early.

qa.q: How might their guide see the plain first version?
qa.a: Their guide sees something that works and can be clicked through, which is more reassuring than a large plan with nothing to demonstrate.

grounding: Shows building a simple working version first, adding later features afterwards, so a demo exists even if time runs short.

subtype: Approach: leaving work to the last month [Pitfall]
passage: Farida, you asked how our project went wrong, so here it is, from me, Mahima. We decided early it was easy: a small app, a small database. "We'll do it in a weekend," someone said, and everyone laughed. So September went by with lunches and cricket. In late October we finally sat down to code. Each of us had written a part, and none of the parts fit. One person's dates were text and another's were numbers, the login broke the reports, and there were four days before submission. We stayed up two nights and got it to work, barely. The viva went badly because we could not explain half the choices. We were confident, and that was the problem.

qa.q: When did the team finally sit down to code?
qa.a: They finally sat down to code in late October.

qa.q: What is Mahima feeling as the project story ends?
qa.a: Mahima feels regret and embarrassment about the rushed submission and the poor viva, adding that being confident was the problem.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the team have used, and why?
qa.a: They could have set small early milestones with dates, because that exposes integration bugs while there is still time to fix them.

qa.q: How might Farida see Mahima's account?
qa.a: Farida, who asked what went wrong, hears an honest story with no excuses, so Farida may feel able to ask about the details too.

grounding: Shows a team assuming the project is easy and delaying the coding until late, then facing integration bugs and a barely working submission.

subtype: Approach: groupthink on the first idea [Pitfall]
passage: At the first meeting, Vinay said, "Fake-review detection. Public dataset from an online shop. Done." He said it so quickly and firmly that everyone nodded, including Ira, though she had never seen such a dataset. Manoj wondered too. Both kept silent, each assuming the others had checked. For three weeks they wrote code against a sample file Vinay had emailed. Then in the canteen Manoj put down his tray. "Ira, can I ask something stupid? Where is the full dataset?" Ira laughed with relief. "I've been looking for two weeks. It doesn't exist." They walked to Vinay's table. He went quiet. Three weeks of work sat on a single small sample, and the deadline was not moving.

qa.q: What topic did Vinay suggest at the first meeting?
qa.a: Vinay suggested fake-review detection using a public dataset from an online shop.

qa.q: What is Ira feeling when Manoj asks about the full dataset?
qa.a: Ira feels relieved, laughing because she has doubted the dataset for weeks and now hears someone else say it.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the team have used at the first meeting, and why?
qa.a: They could have asked everyone to name one worry before deciding, because private doubts come out early when each person is invited to speak.

qa.q: How might Vinay have felt when Ira and Manoj arrive at the table?
qa.a: Vinay probably feels embarrassed and surprised, going quiet when the doubt appears after weeks of work.

grounding: Shows groupthink: the first idea is accepted without questions while two members privately doubt it, and the doubt surfaces only after weeks.

passage:
Madhuri: Ok, before we argue: everyone write ten topic ideas on paper. No talking. 10 min ⏱️
Sachin: Even wild ones?
Madhuri: Especially wild ones. Then we read them all out, no comments
Sachin: Done. 10. One is "bus-delay predictor" 😅
Kirti: Mine: plant disease from leaf photos, library seat finder, exam timetable clash checker...
Madhuri: Great. Now score each 1-5 on: can we finish it, do we care, will our guide approve
Sachin: Wait, I'd never have said mine out loud in a group
Madhuri: That's why paper first 🙂 Pool the scores tonight?
Sachin: Yes. Bus predictor got 4 from me on interest but 2 on feasibility, fair.
Kirti: Leaf photos top so far. Guide meeting on Monday?
Madhuri: Booked.

qa.q: How many topic ideas did each person write?
qa.a: Each person wrote ten topic ideas.

qa.q: What is Sachin feeling about sharing an idea aloud?
qa.a: Sachin feels shy: Sachin says the idea would never have been said out loud in a group, and the paper step allows sharing anyway.

qa.q: What alternative approach could work if the scores end in a tie, and why?
qa.a: They could run a small test of the top two ideas with the guide, because a tie means the scoring cannot separate them and outside input can.

qa.q: How does Kirti experience the process?
qa.a: Kirti reads the ideas from paper and sees the leaf-photo idea come out on top, so the scoring gives Kirti a fair say next to louder voices.

grounding: Shows divergent brainstorming on paper followed by scored voting on feasibility, interest and guide approval so quieter members are heard.

passage: Jatin, let old Gopika tell you about my final-year project, since you say your team is "fine". Our best coder, Sameer, was fast. When a task looked slow, he took it: "Let me just do it, it takes ten minutes." By the third week the rest of us were only making tea and formatting slides. Nobody had lied; it simply felt easier. Then came the viva. The examiner pointed at our code and asked Fatima, "How does this module work?" She looked at Sameer. Silence. Sameer answered for her. The examiner smiled kindly and said, "So who built what?" We passed, but I still remember Fatima's face. I learnt that a project you cannot explain is not really yours.

qa.q: Who was the fast coder in Gopika's team?
qa.a: Sameer was the fast coder.

qa.q: What was Fatima feeling at the viva when the examiner asked about the module?
qa.a: Fatima was embarrassed and helpless, looking at Sameer in silence because she could not explain the code.

qa.q: What choice inside the story could Sameer have made instead of taking tasks over, and why?
qa.a: Sameer could have explained each task and let a teammate try it, because the others would then understand their own part and could answer at the viva.

qa.q: How did the examiner see the team?
qa.a: The examiner saw a group where one person spoke for everyone, which is why the question 'So who built what?' followed.

grounding: Shows one member taking over a team project so the others lose ownership and cannot explain their own work at the viva.

subtype: Approach: negotiating roles by strength and interest [Action]
passage: Hafsa had booked the small seminar room for an hour, and told the team no phones. The four of them sat around the table: Hafsa, Varun, Leela and Dev. "Let's be honest," she began. "What are you hoping to pick up, and where are you already strong?" Varun said he liked databases but froze during presentations. Leela loved design but hated testing. Dev wanted to try machine learning for the first time. Hafsa admitted she was good at organising but had never written a real backend. They filled a table. Each member got a part everyone could see, matching interest and skill, plus a turn reviewing another person's part every Friday. When the hour ended, Varun said, "I actually know what I'm doing now."

qa.q: Which four people were in the meeting?
qa.a: Hafsa, Varun, Leela and Dev were in the meeting.

qa.q: What is Varun feeling as the meeting ends?
qa.a: Varun feels clearer and more confident, saying that he actually knows what he is doing now.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the team use if two people want the same part, and why?
qa.a: They could split it into two pieces or alternate on it, because sharing a popular part lets both learn without anyone losing a visible role.

qa.q: How might Leela see the plan for design and testing?
qa.a: Leela gets the design work Leela loves, and reviewing others' parts gives a small share in testing too, so Leela is not left with testing alone.

grounding: Shows a team negotiating tasks openly by strengths and interests, so each member owns a visible piece and shares a review duty.

subtype: Approach: buffer planning before the viva [Action]
passage: Kishore, you asked what I would tell juniors, so here is my plan, Parul's plan. Our viva was on the 28th. We picked the 14th as our code freeze, and I wrote it on the door of our lab cupboard so nobody could pretend. I said to the team, "Something will slip. It always does. That is why the last two weeks are for testing, writing up, and rehearsing, not for new features." Sure enough, the login bug ate five days. Our friends who had planned to finish on the 27th were coding at midnight before the viva. We were only tired, not panicking. In the rehearsal a senior asked us about our test data, and we had an answer.

qa.q: On which date did the team freeze the code?
qa.a: They froze the code on the 14th.

qa.q: What is Parul feeling as the team runs into the login bug?
qa.a: Parul is tired but steady rather than panicked, because the buffer means a slip can be absorbed.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Parul add if the buffer is still not enough, and why?
qa.a: They could cut the least important feature early, because dropping something planned protects the testing and the rehearsal.

qa.q: How might the friends who planned to finish on the 27th see this plan?
qa.a: They would likely see it as cautious now, but they were the ones coding at midnight, so they might later want the same slack.

grounding: Shows planning to finish coding early and reserving the last two weeks for testing, the report and rehearsal, expecting that something will slip.

subtype: Approach: root-cause analysis of a missed milestone [Revision]
passage: Midterm week was in four days when the second milestone slipped. Salma stood at the board in the project room. "Why did the report module miss its date twice?" Because Manu was late finishing. "Why?" He redid it. "Why?" Because the requirement changed. "Why did it change?" There was a silence. Afreen said slowly, "Because we never wrote down what it should do. Each of us remembered it differently." Salma wrote it on the board: unclear requirement, not laziness. Nobody looked defensive now. Between two study sessions they wrote a single page describing each module and a short list of what "finished" would mean for each module. Then they sent the page to their guide, and the next milestone was met.

qa.q: What did the team write between the study sessions?
qa.a: They wrote a single page describing each module and a short list of what 'finished' would mean for each module.

qa.q: What is Afreen feeling when saying the requirement was never written down?
qa.a: Afreen seems reluctant but honest, speaking slowly because it names a shared mistake rather than blaming Manu.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the team use in future, and why?
qa.a: They could review each requirement together at the start of every milestone, because short check-ins catch differing memories before work is redone.

qa.q: How might Manu see the five-why questions?
qa.a: Manu is asked why he was late and might have felt blamed at first, but the answer shows the cause was the unwritten requirement, so nobody points at Manu.

grounding: Shows root-cause analysis of a missed milestone: repeatedly asking why, finding unclear requirements, and writing a spec with clear completion criteria.
